analysis.one_liner: Rebuilds the wall between regular banks and Wall Street securities firms that the 1999 Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act tore down.
analysis.headline: The bill to re-separate commercial and investment banking was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and died there without a vote in the 118th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the parts of the 1999 Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act that let regular banks merge with or own securities and investment firms, restoring the Glass-Steagall wall that separated insured bank deposits from stock and bond underwriting. Banks would have two years to cut their securities affiliations, securities executives could no longer sit on bank boards, and regulators would be barred from reading the new rules narrowly. The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Financial Services Committee until the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Depositors and taxpayers, who would be insulated from losses if insured banks took big securities risks; borrowers and customers of banks that would refocus on traditional deposit-taking and lending rather than securities speculation. It also benefits smaller banks that cannot afford the same risk-taking as merged financial conglomerates, by leveling the field.

how_it_helps.text: It would bar insured banks from affiliating with securities firms and give regulators and courts the narrowest, most protective reading of that ban, by ratifying the Supreme Court's Investment Company Institute v. Camp interpretation.

It would require securities-firm executives to give up seats on bank boards and existing bank-securities affiliations to be wound down within two years, with extensions capped at one year and each decision reported to Congress.

analysis.who_pays: Large bank holding companies and securities firms, which would have to unwind combined operations, spin off affiliates, and lose the revenue that comes from mixing insured deposits with securities and investment-banking businesses within two years of enactment.

drawbacks.text: The bill would force large bank holding companies to divest investment-bank and securities affiliates within two years, a disruptive restructuring whose costs could be passed on to customers and which would reverse decades of consolidation that some economists argue brought efficiencies and one-stop financial services.

Supporters of the 1999 repeal argue that no major 2008 failure came from a commercial bank's securities affiliation, and that separating banks from securities firms would not by itself have prevented the crisis — so the bill addresses a risk that may be smaller than it appears.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — reducing the odds that taxpayer-insured banks take big trading risks that endanger depositors and require bailouts — is real but hard to quantify, and the cost is also real: repealing parts of Gramm-Leach-Bliley could cut some financial services, raise compliance burdens, and force large banks through a disruptive two-year restructuring. Economists have long disputed how much the Glass-Steagall repeal contributed to the 2008 crisis, since the biggest failures were investment banks and AIG rather than banks that had merged with securities firms. The bill also relies on regulators to police exceptions and extensions. On balance it is a broad insurance policy against a repeat failure, paid for by banks — but the bill itself never advanced, so its practical impact was nil.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on April 19, 2023, referred to the House Financial Services Committee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Marcy Kaptur and seven other House Democrats introduced the Return to Prudent Banking Act of 2023 on April 19, 2023.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, where it remained with no further action.
It drew 15 cosponsors, all of them House Democrats.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without the committee or the House ever voting on the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large bank holding companies and securities firms keep the ability to operate as combined financial conglomerates, with no re-imposed separation between deposit-taking and securities underwriting.

for.name: Marcy Kaptur
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its introduction with seven colleagues.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no action: no hearing, no markup, no report to the House.

against.name: Banking industry
against.role: Large bank holding companies and their trade groups
against.what_they_did: Long opposed reinstating the Glass-Steagall separation; banking industry opposition has been a consistent feature of every effort to revive it.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill never advanced in the Republican-controlled House Financial Services Committee.

industries.industry: Large diversified bank holding companies and securities firms (universal banks)
industries.note: The bill forces them to unwind bank-securities affiliations within two years, ending the merged banking-securities model. For ordinary people, that model is the one whose failures have been backstopped by public deposit insurance and bailouts.

industries.industry: Community and regional banks focused on traditional deposits and lending
industries.note: Banks without securities operations face little direct restriction, and the separation rule applies to their largest competitors; some would benefit from reduced consolidation pressure.

The bill gives agencies new wind-down and exception powers but ties their hands with mandated reports to Congress and strict interpretive limits, reducing discretion they have used to approve bank-securities combinations.
